exam: A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman presents with dysuria and no fever – what is the next step and why? — Obtain urine culture, start nitrofurantoin (safe in pregnancy) to prevent pyelonephritis.
A diabetic patient with a Foley catheter develops fever and flank pain – which investigation is essential? — Blood cultures and urine culture; imaging if obstruction suspected.
You suspect urosepsis in a rural clinic without labs – what immediate actions do you take? — Give IV crystalloids, start empiric ceftriaxone, remove catheter, monitor vitals.
How do you differentiate cystitis from pelvic inflammatory disease on exam? — Absence of cervical motion tenderness and presence of positive urine dipstick favor cystitis.
Why is gentamicin preferred over fluoroquinolones in areas with high resistance? — Local data show >20 % resistance to fluoroquinolones; gentamicin retains activity against common Gram‑negatives.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with UTI – what drug interaction must you watch for? — Avoid co‑administration of trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole if on zidovudine due to marrow suppression.
What are the criteria for classifying a UTI as complicated? — Presence of obstruction, catheter, immunosuppression, pregnancy, renal disease, or systemic signs.
When is imaging mandatory in a patient with suspected pyelonephritis? — When there is no clinical improvement after 48 h, suspicion of obstruction, or atypical presentation.
ai.title: Urological Infections
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Urological infections range from uncomplicated cystitis to life‑threatening urosepsis. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on focused history, bedside exam and limited labs, with prompt treatment to prevent renal damage and sepsis.

b: Most infections are ascending from the urethra.
Gram‑negative bacilli (E. coli) cause >70% of community cases.
Risk factors: catheterisation, obstructive stones, pregnancy, diabetes, HIV, schistosomal urinary tract disease.
sections.p: Infections of the urinary system are common in East Africa, especially among women, children, diabetics, and patients with HIV or schistosomiasis. They may involve the bladder (cystitis), kidneys (pyelonephritis), prostate (prostatitis), or be systemic (urosepsis).

b: Uncomplicated cystitis: dysuria, frequency, no systemic signs.
Complicated infection: obstruction, catheter, immunosuppression, or renal involvement.
Urosepsis: infection plus SIRS (temp >38 °C or <36 °C, HR > 90, RR > 20, WBC > 12 000 or <4 000).
sections.p: Diagnose by integrating symptoms, signs, and simple tests. Severity is staged by systemic response (SIRS criteria) and renal involvement (creatinine rise, imaging).

b: Empirical oral nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for uncomplicated cystitis if available.
IV ceftriaxone or gentamicin for complicated infection or sepsis.
Consider antiretroviral status and possible TB co‑infection in HIV patients.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents renal scarring, sepsis, and death. In low‑resource hospitals, empirical therapy is guided by local resistance patterns and availability of drugs.

t.b: Detects pyuria or nitrite‑producing organisms; positive supports infection when symptoms present.
Identifies causative organism and susceptibility; if culture unavailable, treat empirically based on local patterns.
Assesses renal function; rising creatinine indicates upper‑tract involvement or sepsis‑related AKI.
Indicated in urosepsis; positive culture guides targeted therapy.
Detects obstruction, hydronephrosis, or abscess when imaging is possible; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of obstruction.

b: Urosepsis: aggressive IV fluids, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, monitor vitals, treat source (catheter removal, drainage).
Avoid fluoroquinolones where resistance >20 % or in patients with QT prolongation.
sections.p: Treat the pathogen, relieve obstruction, and support organ function. Choose drugs with activity against common Gram‑negatives and safe in renal impairment.

b: Vaginitis or sexually transmitted infection – vaginal discharge, itching, negative urine dipstick.
Renal colic – flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria, no pyuria.
Pelvic inflammatory disease – lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, positive pregnancy test.
sections.p: Differential diagnoses that mimic urinary infection symptoms.

b: Nitrite negative does not rule out infection (non‑nitrite‑producing organisms).
Pregnant women may have asymptomatic bacteriuria; dipstick can be falsely negative.
Renal impairment can blunt fever response in urosepsis.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation of common tests.

b: Distinguish uncomplicated vs. complicated UTI by risk factors and systemic signs.
Know SIRS criteria for diagnosing urosepsis.
First step in suspected urosepsis: obtain cultures, start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics, and give fluids.
sections.p: High‑yield points for written and oral exams.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever >38 °C with hypotension or altered mental status
Severe flank pain with vomiting suggesting obstructive pyelonephritis
